---
title: "The vein-to-vein database and research extracts"
order: 153
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The short version
- **Finish line:** you can design and govern a recurring research extract from BECS (EXT-21): scope,
  read-only source, linkage keys, transformation, secure transfer, QC and change control, without
  touching a regulated record.
- **Punchline:** the hub's draft data specification arrives, the systems administrator offers the hub
  a login, the medical director wants "everything, monthly." The Director approves **EXT-21 v1 for
  design and test only**: a read-only reporting copy as the source, no external login to anything,
  a data spec cut to what the protocol needs, and a coded donor key held by Lakeshore.
- **The rule in one line:** the extract is a designed product that Lakeshore owns end to end. It is
  not a record, but it reads regulated records, so it runs under change control and never writes back.
- **Monday question:** "Show me EXT-21's last run: the row counts, the reconciliation to BECS
  reports, and who signed off before the file left the building."
- **The trap:** treating "read-only" as a promise. It is a permission set you can show an assessor.
:::

## The draft data specification

The hub's draft data specification lands in RSH-0107's folder as a spreadsheet. It is a field list:
donor demographics at whatever level the spec asks for, donation date, site and procedure, the
donation identification number, component type and manufacturing attributes, and what became of
each component (disposition, and the destination it was distributed to). There are no patient
fields from Lakeshore. Hospitals send patient data. Lakeshore's half of the chain is donor to
component.

Three people react within a day.

The systems administrator, helpful as always: "Easiest thing is to give the hub's data people a
read-only login to the BECS reporting replica. They pull what they want, when they want. We never
build anything."

Your Quality Analyst appears at your desk. "A login for someone outside the company, on a system
that holds every donor? Who decides what they look at? Who proves what they looked at? And what
happens the first time they run a query that locks the thing?"

The medical director, from the hallway: "Just send everything, monthly. If we strip fields now, we'll
regret it when the study team has a new question."

You open RSH-0107. In module 1 you approved participation in principle, with four conditions. Condition
2 was that EXT-21 is read-only. This lesson turns that sentence into a design, and ends with the
decision you record for **EXT-21 version 1**.

## What the program publishes about its database

The program's own description comes from the 2022 design paper (Josephson et al., *Transfusion*;
our local excerpt is in `sources/nih/reds-iv-p-program-design-2022.md`). Everything in this section
is attributed to that paper, and it describes the program as it was written, not the 2026 contract
round. Module 1's note stands: the current round is what people may call "REDS V," but the official
records still describe REDS-IV-P phase 3.

The paper calls the vein-to-vein (V2V) database the backbone of the US program. It holds
information on donors and their donations, the components made from them, and electronic health
record data for patients at participating hospitals. In the paper's words, "Longitudinal databases
for donor/donation, components, and patients/transfusion recipients are linked together so that
blood products can be tracked from donation to transfusion."

On how data arrives, the paper says "donor, donation, component, and patient data are extracted and
transferred to the DCC's Amazon Web Services Virtual Private Cloud using secure data transfer
(sFTP) keys," and that "Submissions are tracked in real-time using dashboards (e.g., dates,
records, ongoing status, QC results)." It adds that the architecture "is based on the Observational
Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) v.6," that data from blood center and
hospital systems "are transformed into the OMOP CDM for analyses," and that "The source data are
retained."

Read what this does and doesn't tell you:

- **It tells you the shape:** extract from the source system, transfer, transform into a common
  model, track quality on dashboards, keep the source.
- **It doesn't tell you the specifics.** Which fields, which cadence, which linkage keys, who does
  the OMOP mapping, what the dashboards flag: all of that lives in the hub's specification and
  agreement, which Lakeshore must ask for and read. The paper is a description of a program, not a
  specification.

If source data are retained for new analyses "without the need for additional data extractions,"
every field you send may live a long time in someone else's environment. That, not slogans, is why
"everything, monthly" is the wrong start. Module 4 follows the data downstream.

## Why the extract is a designed product, and the ITSM bridge

The classic failure is the **accidental service**: a query written for a study gets scheduled, nobody
owns it or documents which BECS field becomes which column, and a later BECS upgrade renames a code
value so the hub's dashboard fills with blanks. Or the query ran under a login that could write, and
one day it does.

The ITSM bridge is the service design package you already know. EXT-21 is a **service**: it has a
customer (the hub, on behalf of the program), a specification (the data spec), an owner, a
configuration (the job, its source connection, its mapping, its keys, its schedule), service levels
(cadence and QC pass criteria), and a change process. The regulated twist is that its source is a
GxP system's data, so "an unowned query" is also a data-integrity risk. The ITIL vocabulary is
service design, configuration management, and change enablement, with a Quality Analyst on the
review.

## The rule in plain English

There is no regulation that says how to build a research extract. What you have is a set of rules
from different tiers that together constrain the design:

1. **The BECS records stay regulated records.** 21 CFR 606.160 says what the records must be and
   how long they are kept. The extract is a derived copy for a research purpose. It does not replace,
   alter or become any of those records. (Module 1, trap 2.)
2. **What leaves Lakeshore should be limited to what the purpose needs.** HIPAA's minimum-necessary
   standard, 45 CFR 164.514(d), asks a covered entity to limit routine disclosures. Whether it
   governs *this* disclosure depends on the pathway the privacy officer confirms in module 3. The
   design habit is the same either way.
3. **Lakeshore's own change control covers the extract.** No source in this course requires a
   research extract to be validated like BECS. Lakeshore's decision is that a scheduled job reading a
   GxP system's data is a configuration item under change control. That is policy, flagged as
   policy.
4. **Nothing external gets inside.** Data goes out through a defined, reviewed, outbound process.
   Nobody outside gets a seat at the source.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it says | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.160(c) | "six-oh-six point one-sixty, c" | Regulation: a donor number relates the unit to the donor and to components from it | Why a unit-level identifier is the linkage backbone |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(1)(vii) | "...b, one, roman seven" | Regulation: donor records relate the donor to each previous donation's unit number | BECS already traces repeat donations; a coded key must preserve that |
| 21 CFR 11.10 | "eleven point ten" | Regulation: controls for closed systems that create, modify, maintain or transmit electronic records | Contrast only: BECS keeps these controls; EXT-21's output is not that record |
| 45 CFR 164.514(d)(3)(i) | "one-sixty-four point five-fourteen, d, three, i" | HIPAA regulation: routine disclosures limited to the amount reasonably necessary | The test every spec field must pass |
| NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3, CM-5 | "eight-hundred fifty-three, CM-3" | Voluntary federal control catalog | Vocabulary for EXT-21 change control |
| FDA, *Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP* (2018) | "FDA's data-integrity Q and A" | Drug-CGMP guidance, not blood | Borrowed only for the reconciliation idea |
| Josephson et al., *Transfusion* 2022 | "the REDS-IV-P design paper" | Peer-reviewed program description | What the program says about its V2V database |

## The actual text

**21 CFR 606.160(c), the identifier that ties a unit to everything else:**

> (c) A donor number shall be assigned to each accepted donor, which relates the unit of blood
> collected to that donor, to his medical record, to any component or blood product from that donor's
> unit of blood, and to all records describing the history and ultimate disposition of these
> products.

*What it means for EXT-21.* The regulation requires BECS to be able to trace unit to donor to
components to disposition. The extract inherits that structure and should not invent a parallel one.
Lakeshore's donation identification number is how a component links back to a donation, and, in the
program's design, how a component linked on the hospital side can be tracked to transfusion. The
paper does not say which identifiers the V2V database links on, so confirm the key list in the hub's
spec. Whether donor identifiers leave Lakeshore, and in what form, is a privacy decision (module 3),
not an IT one.

**45 CFR 164.514(d)(3)(i), from our local excerpt:**

> (3) Implementation specification: Minimum necessary disclosures of protected health information.
> (i) For any type of disclosure that it makes on a routine and recurring basis, a covered entity
> must implement policies and procedures (which may be standard protocols) that limit the
> protected health information disclosed to the amount reasonably necessary to achieve the purpose
> of the disclosure.

*What it means for EXT-21.* A monthly extract is the textbook "routine and recurring" disclosure.
The data spec is the "standard protocol" that limits it. Notice what a hub login would do: the
reader, not Lakeshore, would decide how much to look at. An extract is where you can enforce the
limit, because the extract only contains what you put in it. Whether this paragraph governs
Lakeshore's disclosure depends on the pathway module 3 settles, and this lesson doesn't decide it.
Other pathways have their own rules. See [the HIPAA Privacy Rule](../../healthcare-security-and-privacy/the-hipaa-privacy-rule/index.qmd)
for how minimum necessary works inside a covered entity.

**21 CFR 11.10, opening sentence, as a contrast:**

> Persons who use closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall
> employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, when
> appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records [...]

*What it means for EXT-21.* Those procedures and controls attach to the *records in BECS*: validation,
access limits, audit trails (see [Part 11 for validated systems](../../csv-and-becs/part-11-for-validated-systems/index.qmd)).
EXT-21 reads those records. It does not weaken any of those controls and does not take them over.
The extract file is a derived copy: if it is wrong, the source record is still right, and the fix
is to correct the extract. If the *source* is wrong, the fix is in BECS under BECS's own controls, never
in the extract. Whether the extract file is itself a record under any regulation is a Quality and
regulatory affairs question, flagged in the plan rather than assumed here.

**FDA data-integrity guidance, general thinking only.** It defines data integrity as "the
completeness, consistency, and accuracy of data" and says "System design and controls should enable
easy detection of errors, omissions, and aberrant results throughout the data's life cycle." It is
drug-CGMP guidance, not a blood-establishment rule. Take only the habit: make a missing or distorted
row detectable. See [ALCOA and data integrity](../../data-integrity-and-records/alcoa-and-data-integrity/index.qmd).

**NIST CM-3, voluntary vocabulary.** Two lines carry the weight: "(b) Review proposed
configuration-controlled changes to the system and approve or disapprove such changes with explicit
consideration for security and privacy impact analyses" and "(c) Document configuration change
decisions associated with the system." CM-5 adds "Define, document, approve, and enforce physical
and logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system." Same ideas as the
[release lesson](../../release-management-and-sdlc/release-management-deployment-and-change-control/index.qmd).

## Designing EXT-21, piece by piece

### 1. Scope: the data spec as a negotiated product

Treat the hub's draft as a first offer. For every field, ask five questions and write the answers
next to it:

| Question | Why |
|---|---|
| Which protocol question needs this field? | "Might be useful" is the "everything, monthly" trap |
| Can it be coarser? | Age band instead of birth date, month instead of day, if the protocol allows |
| Does it carry a person's identity? | Donor name, address and contact details are different from component type |
| Where does it live in BECS, and is that a regulated record? | You must know which source field you're mapping |
| What does it cost to keep right? | Every field must be mapped, reconciled, protected and, if asked, corrected |

The medical director's "if we strip fields now, we'll regret it" deserves a real answer: **a
new question is a new version of the spec, not a reason to send everything now.** The spec has a
version number, and adding a field goes through the hub, the privacy officer and change control
(module 1: "new data elements go back to the privacy officer"). A well-run program expects this.
Agreeing that "everything" isn't a spec is not saying no to science.

The medical director agrees once it's framed that way. It costs one meeting, against a possible
retraction later.

### 2. Source: a read-only reporting copy, never production, never a hub login

The systems administrator's instinct fails on four counts, and the Quality Analyst has the first three.

1. **Identity.** An external person inside Lakeshore's systems is an access-management, audit and
   offboarding problem for a research favor.
2. **Control of what is seen.** A login to a replica exposes every table, so minimum-necessary
   discipline has nowhere to stand. The spec is the control point, and a login bypasses it.
3. **Performance risk.** An unfamiliar query can degrade a reporting layer other teams use.
4. **Proof.** "They only read" is a promise. An assessor wants a permission set, an access review
   and logs.

So the decision is the reverse of the instinct. **Lakeshore runs the job, inside Lakeshore, and the
data goes out. Nothing comes in.**

What the source should be:

- **A read-only reporting copy**, not BECS production. The extract's query load, schema changes
  and credentials stay off the live system that supports collection, labeling and release. (Whether
  Lakeshore already has such a copy, and how it is refreshed, is a configuration fact for your CMDB.
  This lesson doesn't invent one.)
- **A dedicated, narrow view over the copy** that exposes only the fields in the approved spec.
  EXT-21's service account can read that view and nothing else.
- **A service account with no write permission anywhere**, enforced in the database's permissions
  and shown to the Quality Analyst as a screenshot or a permission report, not in a README. This is
  the difference between condition 2 in prose and condition 2 in the design.
- **Refresh lag written down.** A copy is behind production by some amount of time. The extract's
  run time and the copy's refresh are part of the design, because a unit's disposition can change
  between the two.

One caution: the reporting copy is still a copy of regulated records. **EXT-21 doesn't make it a
record of record**, and nobody corrects data there. See
[BECS interfaces and data integrity](../../csv-and-becs/becs-interfaces-and-data-integrity/index.qmd)
and [BECS in the pipeline](../../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd).

### 3. Linkage keys: how the pieces find each other

The paper says the databases are "linked together so that blood products can be tracked from
donation to transfusion." For Lakeshore's half, three kinds of key matter.

| Key | What it links | Design question |
|---|---|---|
| **Donation identification number** | A donation to its components, and, on the hospital side, a component to a transfusion | It's the join the program needs. Keep its format exactly as BECS has it, and test for duplicates and orphans every run |
| **Component identifier** | A component to its donation and its disposition | Whatever BECS uses to tell split or pooled products apart should be in the spec, not guessed |
| **Donor key** | Repeat donations by the same donor, across time | Do donor identifiers leave Lakeshore, and in what form? |

The third row is the real design choice, and the privacy officer will have the last word on it (module 3).
IT's job is to lay out the options clearly so she can decide.

| Option | What leaves Lakeshore | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Direct identifiers** | Donor identifiers as they exist in BECS | Simplest linking | Most exposure. Hardest to justify to a privacy officer. Hardest to retract |
| **B. Study-specific coded donor key held by Lakeshore** | A code that means nothing outside Lakeshore. The code-to-donor table (the crosswalk) never leaves | Longitudinal linking works. Lakeshore can re-link for a correction or a legitimate recontact process the agreement permits | You now own a key-management service: generation, protection, backup, retention |
| **C. No donor key at all** | Nothing that ties donations to a donor | Least exposure | Longitudinal donor questions become impossible. Probably incompatible with the program's design |

The Director's v1 design is **B**, with its final form pending module 3. A few design points worth
settling now, labeled as engineering practice rather than regulation:

- **The code is random, not derived.** A "hash of the donor ID" can be recomputed by anyone who
  can guess or hold a list of donor IDs. A randomly assigned code and a protected lookup table
  cannot.
- **The code is stable across runs.** If March's donor 8841 is April's donor 9102, longitudinal
  linking is silently broken.
- **The crosswalk is a sensitive asset.** It lives inside Lakeshore with tight access, is backed up
  and is itself a CMDB item. Losing it is a data-loss problem for the study. Leaking it defeats the
  coding.
- **Coded is not automatically de-identified.** Whether a coded dataset counts as de-identified,
  or as something with its own handling rules, is a legal determination. This curriculum's local
  sources do not include HIPAA's de-identification text, so we don't decide it here. It belongs
  to the privacy officer.

### 4. Transformation and mapping

The paper says data "are transformed into the OMOP CDM." That is a statement about the program's
architecture. Two questions the agreement must answer: **who performs the mapping to OMOP, and
what does Lakeshore send, in what shape?** If the hub or the DCC maps, Lakeshore sends its own
fields in the shape the spec defines.

Either way, Lakeshore owns a document the hub can't write: the **mapping of its own fields**. For
every field in the spec:

- the BECS source (table or report, field) and what it means in Lakeshore's own terms;
- the transformation (units, date formats, truncation, value-set translation, rules for nulls);
- the owner who can answer "what does this value mean?"; and
- the version, because the mapping changes when BECS changes.

Value-set translation deserves a line. BECS's code for a component type or a disposition is
Lakeshore's vocabulary. The spec may use another. The translation table is part of the mapping, and
the unmapped value ("a new code appears that the table has never seen") must be handled by rule, not
by silent default. The standard behavior: stop the run, flag it, resolve it. A fast guess that sends a
plausible but wrong value is worse than a late file.

The OHDSI community, which maintains the OMOP CDM, publishes conversion guidance (the *Book of
OHDSI* ETL chapter is on the resources page). Read it to speak the DCC's language. It is not a
requirement and not a statement of what the DCC will do.

### 5. QC: a checklist and a reconciliation report, every run

The paper says submissions are tracked on dashboards including "QC results." That's the program's
check after the file arrives. EXT-21's own QC is the check **before** it leaves, and every run
produces two documents.

**The QC checklist** (pass or fail per item, a person signs):

- Row counts at each stage: reporting copy, spec view, mapped output, transfer file.
- Required fields populated; values within approved value sets (anything unmapped stops the run).
- Date sanity: no future donations, no component manufactured before its donation.
- Identifier checks: donation identification numbers unique and well-formed; no orphan components or
  donations.
- Coded key checks: every donor coded, no code shared by two donors, no direct identifier anywhere
  in the file.
- File checksum and size recorded before transfer.

**The reconciliation report** compares the extract with BECS's own reports for the same period:
the number of donations, components manufactured by type, components distributed. The extract is a
derived copy, so the question is "does it say what BECS says?" The BECS reports are the reference.
If they disagree, the extract is wrong until proven otherwise. This is the FDA data-integrity
"complete, consistent and accurate" idea, as general thinking.

**A late change in the source** needs a rule written in advance. A disposition can change after a run:
will the next run restate rows, flag changes, or send a full snapshot? The spec decides, EXT-21
does it the same way every time, and the reconciliation report accounts for it.

**The feedback loop.** The DCC's dashboard will report QC results back. Lakeshore keeps an intake
log: date, run, what the dashboard flagged, the cause classified as *extract defect*, *mapping error*,
*spec ambiguity* or *source-data problem*, and the action. The last class matters. **If the cause is
bad data in BECS, nobody fixes it in the extract.** It goes through BECS's normal correction
and deviation processes, and the next run picks up the corrected source. A "fix in the extract" is how a
research job quietly diverges from the regulated record.

### 6. Secure transfer as a process

Module 5 sets the security controls. The process around them belongs in this design:

- **Outbound only.** EXT-21 pushes to the destination the agreement names (the paper describes sFTP
  with keys to the DCC's cloud). Nothing connects in.
- **A named key owner and rotation rule** (module 5).
- **A release step.** The file moves only after the QC checklist is signed. "Send on schedule no
  matter what" is no QC.
- **A transfer log and receipt:** file, checksum, time, confirmation of arrival. No email
  attachments or hand-carried copies.
- **A failure path.** A failed or partial transfer is an incident with a known retry and a known
  contact at the hub.

### 7. Change control for EXT-21 itself

EXT-21 is a scheduled job touching a GxP system's data. The extract is not a regulated record, but
it runs under Lakeshore's change control anyway, for three reasons: it reads regulated data, it
sends data outside, and its mapping depends on something else that changes.

- **Register it in the CMDB**: the job, its schedule, the service account, the view, the
  crosswalk, the mapping document, the transfer credentials and the destination, with owners.
- **Version everything**: spec version, mapping version, code version. A run records which versions
  produced it.
- **Classify changes.** A new field, mapping, destination or cadence is a change with an impact
  analysis, reviewed by the Quality Analyst and, where data content changes, the privacy officer.
- **Never write to BECS.** The permission set proves it. A change that would require a write
  permission is refused and escalated.
- **BECS changes can break EXT-21.** A new BECS release can rename a field, change a code value
  or alter a status. Impact analysis for any BECS change must ask "does this touch an EXT-21 source
  field?" and the CMDB relationship makes that answerable. Module 6 runs exactly this: a BECS
  release breaks the mapping in the same week a rapid-response request arrives.

In NIST's vocabulary this is CM-3, with CM-5's point that who may change the job is enforced. How
much *verification* a research extract needs is a risk-based Lakeshore decision with Quality; no
source we hold prescribes it. The decision below sets a floor: tested, with evidence, before first
real use.

### 8. Testing without real data

Lakeshore's rule from the [environments lesson](../../release-management-and-sdlc/environments-baselines-and-test-data/index.qmd)
applies unchanged: **real donor data lives only in production and validation. Development and test
use synthetic data. Validation holds a de-identified copy.** The first EXT-21 test run uses
the validation environment's de-identified copy, never production data, and its output stays
inside Lakeshore: you review the file, the mapping and the QC report, and you don't transfer it
anywhere until the module 3 conditions clear. Testing the transfer itself needs a destination the
agreement defines. Ask the hub whether a test endpoint exists, and use synthetic content with it.

## See it in one picture

The diagram is EXT-21 as decided: data flows outward through one controlled path, and the dotted
lines are feedback and testing, not access.

```{mermaid}
    R -->|"spec fields only<br/>(approved view)"| J["EXT-21 job<br/>runs inside Lakeshore"]
    K[("Coded donor key crosswalk<br/>held by Lakeshore")] <--> J
    J --> Q{"QC checklist and<br/>reconciliation to BECS reports"}
    Q -->|"fail: hold, investigate"| I["Investigation record"]
    Q -->|"pass: release"| S["Secure transfer: sFTP keys<br/>(per the 2022 paper)"]
    S --> D["Hub / DCC cloud<br/>maps to OMOP CDM"]
    D -.->|"dashboard QC results"| J
    V[("Validation environment:<br/>de-identified copy")] -.->|"first test runs only"| J
    X["Hub login into Lakeshore systems"] -. "refused" .-> P
```

## What an assessor would look for

An FDA inspector cares about EXT-21 only if it could affect the BECS records. A hub site visit, an
IRB, your privacy officer or an internal audit would look at the extract itself:

- **The approved data spec**, versioned, with a rationale per field. Bad answer: "We send what they
  asked for."
- **A permission report** showing the account reads one view and writes nothing. Bad answer: "The
  query only does SELECT."
- **The mapping document** with owner and version. Bad answer: "It's in the script."
- **Signed QC checklists and reconciliation reports** for recent runs. Bad answer: "The DCC would
  tell us."
- **The CMDB record and change history**, including impact analyses for BECS changes.
- **The key-management record** for the coded donor key, and evidence that no outsider holds a
  login to any Lakeshore system.

## Common traps

1. **"It's research, so no change control."** The extract isn't a regulated record, but its source
   is, and a wrong mapping or leaked field is yours.
2. **"A read-only login is the same as an extract."** A login hands over the whole system and leaves
   you to prove what happened. An extract is a defined product you can reconcile.
3. **"The DCC's QC will catch problems."** It sees the file, not BECS, and only after the file left.
4. **"Fix the bad value in the extract."** Source errors are corrected in BECS under its controls.
5. **"Coded means anonymous."** Not necessarily. That is a privacy determination.

## What this means for your job

- **Own the data spec.** Insist on a versioned spec with a purpose for each field, and say no to
  "everything" kindly and in writing.
- **Hold the line on logins.** No external account on any Lakeshore system for this program. The
  answer is a better extract, not a wider door.
- **Ask the Quality Analyst for the proof, not the promise:** the permission report, the last
  reconciliation, the change record.
- **Put EXT-21 in the CMDB with relationships to the BECS fields it reads,** so BECS change
  reviews can ask the question automatically.
- **Treat the coded donor key as a service you now run.** Owner, backup, access review, retention.
- **Escalate when the extract's contents change:** a new field, a new recipient or a new cadence
  goes to the privacy officer before IT builds it.

## The Director's decision for EXT-21 v1

You record this in RSH-0107:

> **EXT-21 version 1 is approved for design and test only. It is not approved to run on production
> data or to transfer anything.**
>
> 1. **Source:** a read-only reporting copy, through a dedicated view containing only specified fields.
>    EXT-21's account has no write permission anywhere.
> 2. **No external login** to any Lakeshore system, for the hub, the DCC or anyone else.
> 3. **Data spec** reduced to what the hub's protocol needs, field by field with a stated purpose.
>    The medical director agrees "everything" is not a specification. New fields come as a new
>    spec version.
> 4. **Donor key:** a coded donor key generated and held by Lakeshore. Its final form is pending
>    the privacy officer's determination (module 3).
> 5. **Every run** produces a QC checklist and a reconciliation report against BECS reports, signed
>    before any release.
> 6. **EXT-21 is registered in the CMDB** and runs under change control, with BECS changes checked
>    for impact on its source fields.
> 7. **First test run** uses the validation environment's de-identified copy, never production data,
>    and no output leaves Lakeshore until the module 3 conditions clear.

Why "design and test only"? RSH-0107's condition 1 (the privacy officer's written pathway) is still
open. Building and testing keeps the relationship moving; running on real data waits for the paper.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The systems administrator says a read-only login for the hub is "less work than building an extract." What are two reasons to refuse it anyway?

Any two of: an external identity inside Lakeshore's systems is an access-management and audit
burden; a login exposes every field, so the minimum-necessary limit has nowhere to be enforced;
unfamiliar queries risk the reporting layer; and "they only read" can't be proven the way a
permission set and logs can. The extract is the control point.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The DCC dashboard shows a spike of components with an impossible manufacturing date. A colleague suggests correcting the dates in the EXT-21 mapping. What is the right path?

First classify the cause. If BECS holds the wrong date, the error is a source-data problem: correct it
through BECS's own controls and let the next run pick it up. If EXT-21 transformed a correct date
wrongly, it's an extract or mapping defect, handled under change control. Silently patching in the
extract leaves two versions of the record.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Does 21 CFR 11.10 require Lakeshore to validate EXT-21 the way it validates BECS?

No source we hold says so. 11.10 applies to systems that create, modify, maintain or transmit
*electronic records* under that rule, and the BECS records keep those controls. Whether the extract
job needs validation-style verification is a risk-based Lakeshore decision with Quality. The
decision here is change control plus tested, evidenced runs. This is a "not a regulatory
requirement, but a policy choice" answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q4: Why is a hash of the donor ID a weak coded donor key?

Anyone who can list or guess donor IDs can recompute the hash and re-link the codes. A randomly
assigned code with a protected crosswalk can't be recomputed. This is engineering practice, not a
regulation, and whether the coded form is acceptable at all is the privacy officer's decision.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q5: Explain to your CIO in two sentences why EXT-21 isn't "just a query."

"EXT-21 is a recurring export of regulated donor and component data to an outside research program,
so it needs a defined data spec, a read-only source, signed quality checks and change control like
any service that touches that system. If it breaks or leaks, the problem lands on Lakeshore and our
regulated records, not on the research program."
:::
